rules.a: Most nationalities need a visa. There are two routes. Consulate route: we issue the invitation letter ($25) for any programme of at least 3 days that includes airport pickup and drop-off. Visa on arrival: if your organised programme includes the Sahara, our Saharan authorisation ($45) lets the visa be issued on arrival at Algiers airport; the arrival stamp is a separate airport fee by length of stay: 1–2 days 5,000 DA (€35), 3–7 days 10,000 DA (€70), 8–10 days 20,000 DA (€140), 11–15 days 25,000 DA (€170), 16–30 days 50,000 DA (€340). If your visa is refused, we refund everything you paid us.
Our guides work in English, French, Spanish, Italian, Arabic, German, Russian. Tell us your language when you enquire and we assign the guide.

Every price you see on the site is the real, fixed price for that tour — it is on each tour page, per person. It covers a private trip or a small group. The only thing that changes it is a custom itinerary or more days than the published programme, which we quote individually; that is rare, and we tell you the figure before you commit.
Our published prices are for private tours and small groups only — we do not run large coach groups. That is what keeps the itineraries flexible: the pace, the stops and the departure date are yours.
We operate all year round, on the dates you choose. We have a large team, so we are not limited to fixed departure dates — tell us when you want to travel and we build the trip around it.

items.a: The Tassili is a plateau reached by a climb, and the sites sit on top of it. That is precisely why the paintings are in the condition they are in, and why the days up there feel like nowhere else in Algeria.

items.q: How old is the rock art?

items.q: Is Algeria safe for tourists?
items.a: Yes for normal tourism in the north and on organised desert trips. Cities are generally calm and welcoming; take the usual precautions you would anywhere. The deep south and border regions are restricted and are visited only with licensed operators and permits.

items.q: Are there areas to avoid?
items.a: The border zones with Mali, Niger, Libya and parts of the far south outside authorised routes are off-limits to independent travel. Organised desert journeys keep to permitted areas with the required authorisations.

items.q: Can I travel independently?
items.a: In the north, yes, with patience and standard care. The Sahara is not for independent travel — it is organised through a licensed Algerian operator with guides, 4x4 and permits.

items.q: Do I need a visa for Algeria?
items.a: Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance at an Algerian consulate, usually supported by an invitation/voucher from a licensed agency. Rules vary by nationality and change over time — always confirm with your consulate.

items.q: Can you help with my visa?
items.a: Yes — as a licensed Algerian operator we provide the invitation letter / tourist voucher ($25) and booking confirmation that most consulates require, with any programme of at least 3 days that includes airport pickup and drop-off. If your programme includes the Sahara, the visa can instead be issued on arrival at Algiers airport ($45 authorisation).

items.q: Is there an e-visa or visa on arrival?
items.a: Generally not for ordinary tourism. The main exception is organised tourism to the far-south desert, where a simplified entry can be arranged for the group. Verify current rules officially before you rely on them.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Algeria?
items.a: Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November) are best for the north — coast, Roman cities and mountains. The Sahara is a winter destination, best from November to February.

items.q: When should I visit the Sahara?
items.a: November to February, when desert temperatures are cool and clear. Summer in the deep south is dangerously hot and not suitable for travel.

items.q: Can I travel during Ramadan?
items.a: Yes — it is a special time to visit, though daytime eating options and some opening hours change. We plan itineraries around it so your trip runs smoothly.

items.q: How much does a trip to Algeria cost?
items.a: It depends on length and style. Our day tours start around €30, multi-day private tours run from a few hundred euros, and our longest, the 14-day Grand Discovery, is €1,850 per person. Each tour page lists its price.

items.q: Is Algeria expensive?
items.a: Day-to-day costs are moderate. The main cost of a trip is private guiding, transport, permits and domestic flights rather than high local prices.

items.q: What do tour prices include?
items.a: It varies by tour — each page has a "What's included / Not included" list. Typically a licensed guide, private transport and some meals or accommodation are included; international flights and visa fees are not.

items.q: How do you get around in Algeria?
items.a: Domestic flights cover the long distances (especially to the Sahara), comfortable trains link the northern cities, and private vehicles with a driver are the easiest way to tour. In the desert, travel is by 4x4 only.

items.q: Do I need to rent a car?
items.a: For the north it is possible, but most visitors prefer a private car and driver. For the south a licensed operator with a properly equipped 4x4 is required — we arrange all transport.

items.q: Are domestic flights reliable?
items.a: Air Algérie and other carriers link Algiers with the main cities and Saharan towns like Djanet and Timimoun. We advise on timings and build flights into your plan (flight cost is usually separate).

items.q: Can I use credit cards and ATMs?
items.a: Algeria is largely a cash economy. Cards are accepted only in some city hotels and rarely elsewhere, and foreign-card ATMs are unreliable. Plan to pay cash for most things.

items.q: What currency is used, and can I get it in advance?
items.a: The Algerian dinar (DZD). It cannot be obtained outside the country, so bring euros or US dollars in cash and exchange them on arrival.

items.q: How much cash should I bring?
items.a: Enough for your personal spending, meals not included in your tour, tips and souvenirs. Bring a mix of larger and smaller notes and keep them secure.

items.q: Is there wifi and mobile data?
items.a: City hotels usually have wifi. A local SIM card (Djezzy, Mobilis or Ooredoo) gives affordable data and is registered with your passport. Coverage thins out quickly in the desert.

items.q: Will my phone work in the Sahara?
items.a: In and around towns, yes. The deep desert is largely off-grid with little or no signal — part of its appeal — so let people know your plans before you head out.

items.q: What is Algerian food like?
items.a: Couscous, slow tagines, grilled meats and coastal fish, fresh bread, Saharan dates, Kabyle olive oil and mint tea poured from a height — Mediterranean and regional, and generous.

items.q: Can you cater for vegetarians or dietary needs?
items.a: Yes — vegetable couscous, salads, pulses and bread make vegetarian eating easy, and we can arrange for allergies or other needs if you tell us in advance.

items.q: Is the tap water safe to drink?
items.a: Stick to bottled water, which is cheap and widely available; it is provided on our desert trips.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for women travellers?
items.a: Generally yes, with normal precautions. Serious harassment is uncommon, but modest dress and awareness — especially outside the big cities — make for a more comfortable trip. Private, guided travel adds an extra layer of ease.

items.q: What should women wear?
items.a: Modest, loosely covering clothing is appreciated; carry a scarf for mosques and conservative areas. Beaches and big-city districts are more relaxed, especially in summer.

items.q: Do I need a permit for the Sahara?
items.a: Yes — the protected desert zones, including Tassili n'Ajjer and the Tadrart, require permits and a licensed local guide. We arrange the permits and guiding as part of any desert trip.

items.q: Can I explore the desert on my own?
items.a: No — independent deep-desert travel is restricted for safety and conservation. It is done with a licensed operator, 4x4 vehicles and the proper authorisations.

items.q: Can I take photos freely?
items.a: Landscapes, monuments and ruins are generally fine. Always ask before photographing people, and avoid photographing military and police sites and some government buildings.

items.q: Can I bring a drone?
items.a: Drones are restricted and often prohibited in Algeria. Do not bring or fly one without explicit prior authorisation — it can cause serious problems at the border or on site.

items.q: Do I need vaccinations?
items.a: No special vaccinations are required for most travellers. Make sure routine vaccinations are up to date and consult your doctor or a travel clinic, and bring any personal medication in its original packaging.

items.q: Is medical care available?
items.a: Cities have hospitals and pharmacies; the desert is remote, so carry a basic personal first-aid kit. Pharmacies are well stocked in towns.

items.q: Do I need travel insurance?
items.a: Yes — we strongly recommend comprehensive travel insurance that covers remote and desert travel. It is not included in tour prices.

items.q: What should I pack for the Sahara?
items.a: Warm layers for genuinely cold desert nights, strong sun protection, a headtorch, sturdy closed shoes, a scarf for sun and dust, and a refillable water bottle.

items.q: What about the cities and the north?
items.a: Comfortable walking shoes for the Casbah and ruins, modest clothing, and a light jacket for spring and autumn evenings. Add swimwear for the coast in summer.

items.q: Is Algeria good for family travel?
items.a: Yes, particularly in the north. The Mediterranean coast, the Roman cities of Tipaza, Djémila and Timgad, and accessible oasis towns all work well with children, and Algerians are exceptionally warm towards families. The main limitation is the deep Sahara, which is demanding for young children.

items.q: Can you take children to the Algerian Sahara?
items.a: Older children and teenagers usually enjoy it, but a deep-desert expedition means long 4x4 days, camping in cold night temperatures and no mobile coverage — hard on toddlers. A good compromise is an accessible oasis town such as Ghardaïa, Timimoun or Bou Saada rather than the Tassili.

items.q: Are there car seats and baby facilities in Algeria?
items.a: Child car seats are rarely provided by rental companies or drivers, so bring your own. Baby-changing facilities are limited outside modern hotels and malls, though nappies, formula and baby food are readily available in city pharmacies and supermarkets.

items.q: What is the best time to visit Algeria with kids?
items.a: Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November) are the most comfortable for the north. Avoid inland summer, when temperatures are punishing, and remember that the desert is a winter destination and cold at night.

items.q: Is Algerian food suitable for children?
items.a: Generally yes. The cuisine is fragrant rather than spicy — couscous, grilled meats, breads, soups and plenty of fresh fruit and pastries suit most children. Use bottled water, and cities have supermarkets for familiar staples.

items.q: Do children need a visa for Algeria?
items.a: Children need their own visa on the same basis as adults, with their own passport and application. Requirements vary by consulate and some ask for additional documentation for minors, so start the process early — see our visa guide.

items.q: Can you travel to Algeria during Ramadan?
items.a: Yes, and it can be a memorable time to visit. Sites and tours generally operate, though opening hours shift and many cafés and restaurants close during daylight. Cities become lively after sunset with iftar, and hospitality is at its warmest. Travellers are not expected to fast, but eating and drinking discreetly in public during the day is the respectful approach.

items.q: What are the public holidays in Algeria?
items.a: Fixed national holidays are New Year's Day (1 January), Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year (12 January), Labour Day (1 May), Independence Day (5 July) and Revolution Day (1 November). Islamic holidays — Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, the Islamic New Year, Ashura and Mawlid — follow the lunar calendar and move each year.

items.q: Is Christmas celebrated in Algeria?
items.a: Christmas is not a public holiday in Algeria, which is a majority-Muslim country, and 25 December is a normal working day. Small Christian communities do mark it, and churches such as the Sacré-Cœur Cathedral and Notre-Dame d'Afrique in Algiers, as well as churches in Oran and Constantine, hold services.

items.q: What happens during Eid in Algeria?
items.a: Eid al-Fitr, at the end of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha are the two biggest family holidays. Expect widespread closures of shops and offices for one to two days, special morning prayers, family gatherings and heavy domestic travel. Book transport and accommodation well ahead if your trip overlaps.

items.q: What is Yennayer?
items.a: Yennayer is the Amazigh (Berber) New Year, marked on 12 January and recognised as a national public holiday in Algeria. It is celebrated with traditional meals and family gatherings, and is especially prominent in Kabylie, the Aurès and the M'Zab.

items.q: Should I avoid visiting Algeria during religious holidays?
items.a: Not necessarily. Ramadan and the Eids offer real cultural depth, and tours still run. The practical trade-offs are shifting opening hours, reduced daytime dining during Ramadan, and closures plus busy transport around the Eids. If your itinerary is tight, plan around the Eid days.

items.q: How many days do you need in Algeria?
items.a: Allow 10–14 days for a first trip that combines the Roman north with one desert region. A focused week is enough if you stay in the north around Algiers and the eastern Roman cities.

items.q: Is 7 days enough for Algeria?
items.a: Yes, for one region. A week comfortably covers Algiers, a stretch of coast and the eastern Roman cities (Constantine, Timgad, Djémila). It is not enough to add the deep Sahara.

items.q: What is the best 10-day Algeria itinerary?
items.a: Spend the first half in and around Algiers and the eastern Roman circuit, then use the second half for either the Andalusian west (Tlemcen and Oran) or the M'Zab valley oasis towns, depending on your interests.

items.q: Can you visit the Sahara and the north in one trip?
items.a: Yes, on a 14-day itinerary: do the Roman north first, then fly south to Djanet or Tamanrasset for a guided 4x4 leg in the Tassili n'Ajjer or Hoggar. Keep it to the November–February window.

items.q: Do you need a guide for an Algeria itinerary?
items.a: Not in the north, where you can travel independently with patience. The deep south requires a licensed guide, 4x4 transport and permits, so those legs are arranged through an operator.

items.q: What should I wear in Algeria?
items.a: Modest, comfortable clothing that covers shoulders and knees, especially outside big cities. Lightweight layers work best: warm days, cooler evenings, and cold desert nights. A headscarf is useful for women, particularly in the south and at religious sites.

items.q: What do I need to pack for the Algerian Sahara?
items.a: Warm layers for cold nights, strong sun protection (hat, sunglasses, high-SPF), a headscarf against sand and sun, sturdy closed shoes, a refillable water bottle, and a power bank. Nights in the desert can be genuinely cold.

items.q: Should I bring cash to Algeria?
items.a: Yes — cash is essential. Card acceptance is limited outside major hotels and ATMs can be unreliable. Bring euros or dollars to change, and keep dinars for daily spending.

items.q: Do I need a power adapter for Algeria?
items.a: Algeria uses European-style type C and F plugs at 230V. Bring a suitable adapter and, for the desert, a power bank since electricity is limited on expeditions.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for tourists?
items.a: For ordinary travel the northern cities, the Roman east, the western heritage towns and the organised south are generally safe; petty theft in crowds is the main concern. Some border and remote desert areas carry official warnings.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for women travellers?
items.a: Generally yes, with the usual precautions. Modest dress is respectful and reduces unwanted attention; many women travel solo without incident, especially in cities.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for families?
items.a: Yes — the coast, the cities and accessible Roman sites suit families well. Manage heat, water and sun, especially near the desert.

items.q: Which areas should I avoid in Algeria?
items.a: Remote border zones near Mali, Niger and Libya, and some far-desert areas, are commonly advised against. Check your government's current map-based advisory.

items.q: Is it safe to drive in Algeria?
items.a: Main roads are generally good but driving standards and night-time hazards mean caution is wise; many visitors prefer a driver. Avoid night driving on rural routes.

items.q: Is the Algerian Sahara safe to visit?
items.a: Yes, when travelled with a licensed operator who arranges guides and permits and keeps to authorised areas. Independent deep-desert travel is restricted.

items.q: What are the main risks for tourists?
items.a: Petty theft in crowded places, road-traffic risk, and desert heat — far more than any threat of violence against visitors in the main regions.

items.q: Are there scams to watch for?
items.a: The usual: overcharging, unofficial 'guides', and currency-exchange tricks. Agree prices first, use reputable operators, and understand the official versus parallel exchange rate.

items.q: What are the emergency numbers in Algeria?
items.a: Police 17, Civil Protection (fire/rescue) 14, Gendarmerie 1055, and SAMU medical 115 — confirm locally, as numbers can vary.

items.q: Can I buy a SIM card in Algeria as a tourist?
items.a: Yes. Djezzy, Mobilis and Ooredoo all sell prepaid SIM cards to visitors. You must show your passport to register the line, which is a legal requirement, and you can buy at the airport or at operator shops in any city.

items.q: Is internet good in Algeria?
items.a: In the northern cities the 4G mobile internet is generally good and cheap. Coverage weakens in mountain areas and is effectively absent in the deep Sahara. Fixed and hotel Wi-Fi exists widely but is often slow, so mobile data is usually the better option.

items.q: Does my phone work in the Algerian Sahara?
items.a: Not in the deep desert. There is no mobile coverage across the Tassili, the Tadrart or most of the Hoggar. Guided expeditions carry satellite communication, and you should download offline maps and warn family that you will be uncontactable.

items.q: Does eSIM work in Algeria?
items.a: Support is limited and depends on your provider and handset. A physical local prepaid SIM remains the reliable default for visitors; check with your operator before relying on eSIM alone.

items.q: How much does mobile data cost in Algeria?
items.a: Prepaid data bundles are inexpensive by European or North American standards, and the three operators compete on tourist-friendly packages. Buying locally is far cheaper than international roaming.

items.q: Does it snow in Algeria?
items.a: Yes. The Atlas mountains get real winter snow, including Chréa above Blida, the Djurdjura range around Tikjda in Kabylie, and the Aurès mountains. Snow typically falls between December and March, and the high plateaus around Sétif and Batna also see cold, occasionally snowy winters.

items.q: Can you ski in Algeria?
items.a: There are small ski stations at Chréa, in the mountains above Blida about an hour from Algiers, and at Tikjda in the Djurdjura. They are modest facilities rather than alpine resorts, but skiing and snow days are genuinely possible in a good winter.

items.q: Can you see snow and the Sahara on the same trip?
items.a: Yes, in winter. Because Algeria stacks Mediterranean coast, mountains, high plateaus and desert, you can walk in cedar-forest snow near Blida and, after a short domestic flight south, stand among warm Saharan dunes within the same week.

items.q: What is the best month for the snow-and-Sahara contrast?
items.a: December to February. That window overlaps the mountain snow season with the prime Saharan season, when desert days are warm and nights are clear and cold. By spring the snow has mostly gone; by summer the deep desert is unsafe.

items.q: How cold does it get in Algeria?
items.a: Mountain areas fall to around or below freezing in winter, with snow. The northern coast stays mild at roughly 10–17°C. Saharan days are warm, often 20–25°C, but desert nights can drop close to freezing, which surprises most visitors.

items.q: What is the best way to get around Algeria?
items.a: Fly for long distances (especially to the Sahara), use trains and buses between northern cities, shared taxis for shorter hops, and a guided 4x4 for the desert.

items.q: Are there domestic flights in Algeria?
items.a: Yes. Air Algérie and other carriers link Algiers, Oran and Constantine with each other and with southern towns such as Djanet, Tamanrasset and Ghardaïa. Book ahead, as southern frequencies are limited.

items.q: Does Algeria have trains?
items.a: Yes — the national operator SNTF runs intercity services across the north, comfortable on the main lines, plus suburban services around Algiers.

items.q: How do shared taxis (louages) work?
items.a: They run fixed town-to-town routes, leave when full, and are paid in cash. They are flexible and cheap but less predictable than buses.

items.q: Can I rent a car in Algeria?
items.a: Yes, mainly in cities and at airports. It suits the north; for the desert, use a licensed operator with a 4x4 rather than self-driving.

items.q: How do I get to the Sahara?
items.a: Fly to a southern gateway such as Djanet or Tamanrasset, then travel by guided 4x4 arranged by a licensed operator who handles permits.

items.q: Is public transport good in Algerian cities?
items.a: The big cities are well served: Algiers has a metro and tram, and Oran, Constantine, Sétif and others have modern, cheap trams.

items.q: How much does transport cost in Algeria?
items.a: City rides cost under €1; intercity buses and trains are inexpensive; domestic flights are the priciest common option. The exchange rate affects real costs, so confirm when booking.

items.q: Is Algeria expensive to travel?
items.a: No, not for food and local transport, which are cheap by European standards. Comfortable hotels are mid-priced and guided Saharan trips are the expensive part. A mid-range traveller in the north spends about €50–100 a day excluding international flights.

items.q: How much money do you need per day in Algeria?
items.a: Budget travellers in the north can manage on roughly €25–45 a day; mid-range travellers spend about €50–100. A guided deep-desert expedition runs far higher — around €130–260+ a day once guides, 4x4s and permits are included.

items.q: Should I use cash or card in Algeria?
items.a: Carry cash. Card acceptance is limited outside major-city hotels and ATMs can be unreliable, so bring dinars and some euros or dollars to change.

items.q: Why does the exchange rate matter so much in Algeria?
items.a: Algeria has an official exchange rate and a widely-used parallel rate, and the difference is significant. Changing hard currency locally can stretch a travel budget considerably, so it's worth understanding before you arrive.

items.q: What is the most expensive part of an Algeria trip?
items.a: After international flights, the guided Sahara is the biggest cost, because it involves licensed guides, 4x4 transport, permits and internal flights. The northern part of a trip is comparatively affordable.

items.q: Do I need a visa to visit Algeria?
items.a: Most nationalities do and must apply in advance at an Algerian consulate. A small number are exempt; confirm your status with the consulate that serves you.

items.q: Is there a visa on arrival or e-visa for Algeria?
items.a: Generally no for independent tourists. Organised tours that include the Sahara can use a visa on arrival at Algiers airport, arranged by a licensed Algerian agency; any e-visa pilots change, so verify officially.

items.q: What documents do I need for an Algeria tourist visa?
items.a: Typically a valid passport, completed form, photos, proof of accommodation or an agency invitation, a return ticket and proof of funds — plus anything the specific consulate requires.

items.q: How long does an Algeria visa take?
items.a: Often a few days to several weeks depending on the consulate and season. Apply early.

items.q: How much does an Algeria visa cost?
items.a: Fees vary by nationality and consulate and change over time, so confirm the current fee officially rather than relying on figures online.

items.q: Do I need an invitation letter or voucher?
items.a: Tourist applications commonly require a hotel booking or an invitation/voucher from a registered Algerian travel agency; business visas need a company invitation.

items.q: Where should I apply?
items.a: At the Algerian consulate or embassy responsible for your country of residence; jurisdictions are by where you live.

items.q: Why are Algeria visa applications refused?
items.a: Most refusals are administrative — incomplete documents, missing accommodation proof, insufficient funds or inconsistent travel plans. A complete, consistent file is the best safeguard.

items.q: Is Algeria or Morocco better to visit?
items.a: Morocco is easier and better developed for tourism, with famous souks and riads. Algeria is wilder and far less visited, with better-preserved Roman cities and a vaster, more pristine Sahara. Choose based on whether you want ease (Morocco) or depth and space (Algeria).

items.q: Is Algeria cheaper than Morocco?
items.a: Day-to-day costs (food, local transport) are low in both. Algeria can be very affordable in the north, but guided Saharan trips are the main expense; Morocco has more budget-to-luxury range because its tourism is more developed.

items.q: Is Algeria harder to visit than Morocco?
items.a: Somewhat. Most nationalities need a visa for Algeria arranged in advance, tourism infrastructure is lighter, and the deep south needs a licensed operator. Morocco is easier for independent first-timers.

items.q: Which has a better Sahara, Algeria or Morocco?
items.a: For sheer scale and remoteness, Algeria — the Tassili n'Ajjer and the Tadrart are world-class and uncrowded. Morocco's Merzouga dunes are more accessible and set up for tourism.

items.q: Is Algeria or Tunisia better to visit?
items.a: Tunisia is easier and better set up for tourism, with visa-free entry for many nationalities, short flights from Europe and resort beaches. Algeria is far less visited and rewards travellers who want depth: better-preserved Roman cities and a much larger, wilder Sahara.

items.q: Is Algeria cheaper than Tunisia?
items.a: Day-to-day costs are low in both. Tunisia has more competition in hotels and packages, so all-in holidays can be very cheap. In Algeria the north is affordable but guided Saharan expeditions are the big expense.

items.q: Which has better Roman ruins, Algeria or Tunisia?
items.a: Both are outstanding. Algeria's Timgad and Djémila are among the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere and see very few visitors; Tunisia's Carthage and the amphitheatre at El Djem are world-class and far more visited.

items.q: Which is easier for a first trip to North Africa?
items.a: Tunisia. It is visa-free for many nationalities, has short flights from Europe, more hotels and an established tourist circuit. Algeria needs more planning — a visa in advance and a licensed operator for the deep south.

items.q: Which has a better Sahara experience?
items.a: Algeria, for scale and remoteness — the Tassili n'Ajjer and Tadrart are vast, uncrowded and rich in prehistoric rock art. Tunisia's desert around Douz and Tozeur is more accessible and easier to visit briefly.

items.q: What is the national dish of Algeria?
items.a: Couscous — steamed semolina with a meat-and-vegetable broth — traditionally eaten on Fridays and at celebrations.

items.q: Is it easy to be vegetarian?
items.a: Reasonably — salads, soups, bread and vegetable couscous are common, though many broths are meat-based.

items.q: Where can I buy authentic Algerian handicrafts?
items.a: Regional markets and cooperatives — Ghardaïa for pottery and brass, Kabylie for ceramics and silver, southern souks for Tuareg leather.

items.q: Is bargaining expected?
items.a: Yes, gentle bargaining is normal — but stay fair to the makers.

items.q: What is the best time to visit the Algerian Sahara?
items.a: November to February, when daytime temperatures are cool. Avoid June–August.

items.q: Do I need a permit?
items.a: Yes — deep-desert areas require permits and a licensed guide, normally arranged through an organised tour.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Algeria overall?
items.a: Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November), when the north is comfortable and the desert edges are pleasant.

items.q: When should I visit the Algerian Sahara?
items.a: November to February, when days are clear and cool. Avoid the deep desert in summer, when heat is dangerous.

items.q: When is the coast best?
items.a: May to October for warm sea and beach weather, peaking in July and August.

items.q: What months should I avoid?
items.a: June–August for inland and desert travel due to extreme heat; mid-winter if you specifically want to swim.

items.q: Can I trek in the mountains?
items.a: Yes, roughly May–October; the Djurdjura and Aurès can be snowy in mid-winter.

items.q: How does Ramadan affect travel?
items.a: Dates shift each year; daytime hours are quieter with many places opening after sunset. It can be a rewarding, if slower, time to visit.

items.q: Is spring or autumn better?
items.a: Both are excellent; spring brings a greener north, autumn brings warm seas and stable desert-edge weather.

items.q: When is best for photography?
items.a: The cool desert months (Nov–Feb) for the Sahara, and the clear shoulder seasons for the north.

items.q: Can you spend Christmas in Algeria?
items.a: Yes, and it is a rewarding time to go. Christmas is not a public holiday in Algeria, so everything operates normally and there are no festive crowds or price surges. Late December is also the prime season for the Sahara, with warm days and clear nights, while the north stays mild. Churches in Algiers, Oran and Constantine hold Christmas services for visitors who want to attend.

items.q: Is Algeria a good winter sun destination?
items.a: For desert travel, yes. December and January bring warm daytime temperatures in the Sahara — often 20–25°C — with cold, clear nights, while the Mediterranean north stays mild and green at roughly 10–17°C. It is not a beach-swimming destination in winter.

items.q: What is the weather like in Algeria in December?
items.a: The northern coast is mild and fairly wet, around 10–17°C. The Atlas mountains can be snowy. The Sahara is dry with warm days, often 20–25°C, and cold nights that can fall near freezing.

items.q: Are there Christmas celebrations in Algeria?
items.a: Not publicly, in the commercial sense — there are no Christmas markets, and 25 December is a working day. Algeria's small Christian community marks it with church services, including at the Sacré-Cœur Cathedral and Notre-Dame d'Afrique in Algiers, and in Oran and Constantine.

items.q: Is New Year a holiday in Algeria?
items.a: Yes, 1 January is a public holiday. Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, is also a national holiday on 12 January, so a trip spanning late December into January can take in both.

items.q: What should I pack for Algeria at Christmas?
items.a: Layers for a mild, sometimes wet north, and genuinely warm clothing for desert nights, which can drop close to freezing. Add sun protection for bright desert days and sturdy shoes for mountain or dune walking.

items.q: How many days do you need in Algeria?
items.a: Allow 10–14 days to combine the Roman north, a city or two and one desert region; a week suits a focused northern trip.

items.q: Can I travel independently in Algeria?
items.a: Yes in the north, with patience; the deep Sahara requires licensed guides, 4x4 transport and permits.

items.q: What should I not miss in Algeria?
items.a: The Roman cities of Timgad and Djémila, the Casbah of Algiers, the M'Zab valley, and the Tassili n'Ajjer if you reach the south.

items.q: Is alcohol available in Algeria?
items.a: Algeria is a majority-Muslim country; alcohol is available in some hotels and licensed venues but is not widespread. Dress and behave modestly, especially outside cities.

items.q: Do I need cash or cards?
items.a: Carry cash (dinars). ATMs exist in cities but card acceptance is limited; bring some euros to change.

items.q: Is Djanet or Timimoun better for a first trip to the Sahara?
items.a: Timimoun is the easier first taste: warm guesthouse nights, short excursions and a lot of culture. Djanet is the stronger desert experience — the landscapes and rock art most people picture when they think of the Sahara — and it is perfectly manageable for anyone reasonably fit on our 4×4 itineraries.

items.q: How much does a trip to Djanet or Timimoun cost?
items.a: With Algeria Compass, our 5-day Djanet Sahara Safari is from €828 per person, the 7-day Tadrart Rouge and Ihrir circuits from €920 with the return flight from Algiers included, and the 7-day Sefar trek from €1,120. The 5-day Timimoun Desert Escape is from €492 per person.

items.q: When is the best time to visit Djanet and Timimoun?
items.a: October to April for both. November to February gives the clearest, coolest days in the desert; nights are cold. The deep south is not travelled in summer.

items.q: Do you sleep in tents in Djanet?
items.a: On our Djanet trips, yes — most nights are in desert camps or wild bivouac, with tents, mattresses and blankets provided, and some travellers choose to sleep in the open. In Timimoun you stay in a guesthouse every night.

items.q: Can I visit both Djanet and Timimoun on one trip?
items.a: Yes, with ten days or more. They are far apart in the Sahara, so the link is by air rather than road; we plan the flights and dates around your trip.

items.q: Are there five-star hotels in Algeria?
items.a: Yes, in the northern cities. Algiers has the widest choice, with international-brand hotels, and there are comparable properties in Oran and Constantine. Outside those cities the standard drops to good local hotels, and in the Sahara the equivalent of five-star is a well-equipped private camp with proper bedding, catering and vehicle support — there is no design-lodge market of the kind Morocco and Oman have.

items.q: How much does a luxury trip to Algeria cost?
items.a: Our all-inclusive eight-day 5-Star Collection journeys start at €1,615 per person, covering internal flights, five-star hotels, all meals, a private 4WD fleet, guides and UNESCO entry fees. Shorter private tours run from about €200 per person, and private guided day tours from €30. Every tour page carries its own fixed price.

items.q: What makes travel in Algeria luxurious if the hotels are not the draw?
items.a: Exclusivity. Timgad, Djémila and Tipaza are among the best-preserved Roman cities in the world and you will often walk them with nobody else there. Add a private vehicle fleet, a tour leader who stays with your group throughout, expert local guides at each site, and the logistics — permits, internal flights, visa paperwork — taken off your hands entirely.

items.q: Are your tours private, or do we join a group?
items.a: Private only. Our published prices are for private trips and small groups, your own party, on the dates you choose. We do not run large coach groups, and we have no fixed departure dates.

items.q: Can you arrange a private jet or helicopter transfer?
items.a: Domestic aviation in Algeria is tightly regulated and charter is not a routine tourism product here, so treat any operator promising it casually with caution. Tell us what you have in mind and we will tell you honestly what is and is not possible on your dates.

items.q: Is the Algerian Sahara comfortable at the top end?
items.a: It is comfortable, but it is camping — a serviced private camp with proper bedding, a cook, vehicle support, water and communications, on authorised routes with a licensed guide. Nights between November and February are genuinely cold. What it offers instead of a suite is silence, dark skies and the Tassili and Tadrart largely to yourself.

items.q: How far ahead should a luxury trip to Algeria be booked?
items.a: Allow two to three months. The visa alone can take from two weeks to over a month depending on your consulate, southern flights are thin and sell out, and Sahara permits take time. Trips do come together faster, but that is the comfortable window.

items.q: How do I tell a serious Algerian operator from a reseller?
items.a: Ask three questions: who holds the Algerian operating licence, who physically meets you at the airport, and who applies for your Sahara permits. If the answers point to a third company, you are buying a resold product with a margin on top and less control when something moves.

items.q: Is the M'Zab Valley a UNESCO site?
items.a: Yes — the M'Zab Valley was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1982 as an outstanding traditional human settlement adapted to the desert.

items.q: Why did Le Corbusier admire the M'Zab Valley?
items.a: He studied its egalitarian, climate-adapted design — cubic terraced houses, shaded streets and a communal water system — and drew on those principles in his own modern architecture.

items.q: Is Algeria safe for solo female travellers?
items.a: Generally yes, with common-sense precautions. The north and usual tourist routes are welcoming. Foreign women may attract attention and occasional low-level harassment, but serious incidents are uncommon and many women travel Algeria solo without problems.

items.q: What should a woman wear in Algeria?
items.a: Modest, comfortable clothing that covers shoulders and knees, especially outside big cities. A scarf is useful for sun, sand and religious sites. Modest dress noticeably reduces unwanted attention.

items.q: Can a woman travel to the Algerian Sahara alone?
items.a: The deep Sahara requires a licensed operator, guide and 4x4 for everyone, regardless of gender. Within that guided setup it's a safe, well-organised experience; you don't travel the deep south independently.

items.q: How do women handle harassment in Algeria?
items.a: Low-level attention (comments, staring) can occur. Projecting confidence, avoiding eye contact with persistent men, dressing modestly, and staying in busier areas all help. Serious harassment is uncommon, and a local guide adds a layer of ease.

items.q: What is the difference between the Tadrart Rouge and the Tassili n'Ajjer?
items.a: The Tassili n'Ajjer is the great sandstone plateau and protected area around Djanet, famous for its prehistoric rock art. The Tadrart Rouge lies to its south-east, toward the Libyan border, and is known for pink dunes, red rock and natural arches. On our trips the Tadrart and Ihrir circuits are travelled by 4×4; the high plateau at Sefar can only be reached on foot.

items.q: Which Djanet trip is best for a first visit?
items.a: The Tadrart Rouge. It has the landscapes most people come for, famous engravings, and an easy pace by 4×4. Choose Ihrir if you have seen dunes before and want something unexpected, and Sefar if you are a keen walker who cares most about the rock paintings.

items.q: How fit do you need to be for the Sefar trek?
items.a: Reasonably fit and used to walking: 4 to 7 hours a day, with about 500 metres of ascent on the first day to get onto the plateau. Guides, cooks and donkey handlers carry the camp, so you only carry a day pack.

items.q: Are flights included on the Djanet trips?
items.a: On the three 7-day journeys — Tadrart Rouge, Ihrir and Sefar — yes: the return Air Algérie flight from Algiers to Djanet and every airport transfer are included. The 5-day Djanet Sahara Safari starts and ends in Djanet, so the flight is not included.

items.q: Can you swim at Ihrir?
items.a: Sometimes. The pools of Oued Essendilène can be swum in depending on the season — bring something to swim in, and your guide will tell you on the day.

items.q: What is Algeria most famous for?
items.a: Algeria is famous for its Sahara — the largest in the world within one country — its exceptionally well-preserved Roman cities like Timgad and Djémila, the UNESCO Casbah of Algiers, and the rock art of the Tassili n'Ajjer.

items.q: What should you not miss in Algeria?
items.a: Don't miss the Roman cities of Timgad and Djémila, the Casbah of Algiers, the M'Zab valley oasis towns, coastal Tipaza, and — if you reach the south — the Tassili n'Ajjer.

items.q: How many UNESCO sites does Algeria have?
items.a: Algeria has seven UNESCO World Heritage sites: Timgad, Djémila, Tipaza, the Casbah of Algiers, the M'Zab Valley, Beni Hammad Fort, and the Tassili n'Ajjer.

items.q: Is the Algerian Sahara worth visiting?
items.a: Yes — the Tassili n'Ajjer and the Tadrart are among the world's great deserts, with prehistoric rock art, sandstone arches and dunes. It's a guided, winter, permit-based expedition.

tours.t: Ihrir & the Tassili — 7 Days of Oases and Ergs
tours.w: Ihrir & the Tassili — 7 Days of Oases and Ergs Everyone expects the Sahara to be dry. Ihrir is where it is not — a sunken oasis of standing water, reeds and rock pools, an hour from dunes that run to the horizon. The greener Tassili: the water-filled gueltas of Ihrir, the Essendilène canyon, Erg Admer dunes and Tikoubaouine. Flights and transfers included. If the Tadrart is the Sahara of sand, Ihrir is the Sahara of water. This circuit works the northern side of the Tassili n’Ajjer: an enclosed oasis whose gueltas hold water year-round, a canyon you can swim in when the season allows, wind-sculpted rock towers at Tikoubaouine, and the high dunes of Erg Admer for sunset. tours.w: Sefar Trek — Into the Tassili Plateau on Foot You cannot drive to Sefar. You climb to it, and you walk for days between painted walls that are five to eight thousand years old. A seven-day walking expedition onto the Tassili plateau to Sefar — the greatest open-air gallery of prehistoric painting in the Sahara. Flights included. This is the serious one. From Djanet the track climbs onto the Tassili plateau, and from there everything moves at walking pace — guides, cooks and donkey handlers carrying the camp while you cover five to seven hours a day between rock-art sites. Tin Zoumaitek and the valley of millennial cypresses, the painted 'dancers' of Tin Tazarift, the masks of Sefar Noir and the great gods of Sefar Blanc, and finally Djabarren, the largest single ensemble of paintings in the Tassili. This is the whole country in one journey, sequenced so that every internal flight is a scheduled direct service — no transits, no lost days in airports.
